noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate the evolution of carbon dioxide and heat from respiring seeds or other suitable living organisms

primer.text: Respiration is invisible, so practicals make it obvious. Two classic set-ups use germinating seeds: one traps the carbon dioxide they release in limewater, the other watches a thermometer climb as heat escapes respiring life. This note rehearses both, plus the CORMS habit that turns a result into a mark.

lessons.title: Trapping the Carbon Dioxide
sourceHeadings: Practical investigation: demonstrating the production of carbon dioxide from respiration
lessons.opening: Three matched tubes hold germinating seeds, boiled seeds and glass beads; each vents through a delivery tube into a little limewater, and only the living seeds should cloud their indicator.
keyPoints: Tube A holds germinating seeds, tube B boiled seeds, tube C glass beads.
Each seed tube connects to a boiling tube holding limewater.
The delivery tube dips just below the limewater surface.
Warm conditions around 25-30 degrees Celsius speed respiration overnight.
Only living material releases enough carbon dioxide to cloud limewater.

low.restatement: Living seeds cloud the limewater; dead seeds and beads leave it clear.
low.analogy: Breathing into limewater fogs it — the same cloudy sign as the classic blow-through demonstration.
low.examPointer: Name limewater as calcium hydroxide if asked for the indicator chemical.

medium.restatement: The boiled and bead tubes are controls: they prove the colour change tracks respiration, not the apparatus or the cotton wool.
medium.analogy: A placebo arm in a drug trial — without the control tubes, the claim has no baseline.
medium.examPointer: Offer hydrogen-carbonate indicator as the orange-to-yellow alternative when any suitable indicator is allowed.

check.stem: Which tube should turn limewater cloudy?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Boiled seeds are dead and stop respiring.
Beads contain no living material at all.
Only the respiring seeds release enough carbon dioxide.

check.stem: What does limewater become when carbon dioxide passes through it?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Pink belongs to phenolphthalein, not this test.
Blue belongs to copper compounds, not this indicator.
That shift belongs to hydrogen-carbonate indicator.

check.stem: Why are glass beads included as a third tube?

options.text: To match the volume of the other tubes without adding anything living
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To feed the seeds during the run
options.explanation: Beads are inert and feed nothing.
Absorbing the gas would hide the result.
Beads cannot respire or catalyse anything.

check.stem: Why is the delivery tube's end held just below the limewater surface?

options.text: So released gas bubbles through the limewater and reacts with it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Evaporation is not the concern; contact is.
The test is qualitative cloudiness, not volume.
The seeds sit separately in their own tube.

check.stem: Which alternative indicator turns from orange toward yellow as carbon dioxide accumulates?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Iodine signals starch, not this gas.
Universal indicator tracks pH broadly, not carbon dioxide specifically.
Litmus shows acidity roughly, but the named reagent here is hydrogen-carbonate.

check.stem: State the volume of limewater poured into each boiling tube.
check.modelAnswer: Two cubic centimetres of limewater go into the bottom of each tube.

check.stem: Name the chemical dissolved in limewater.
check.modelAnswer: Limewater is calcium hydroxide dissolved in water.

check.stem: Explain why the boiled-seed tube is essential to the carbon dioxide investigation.
check.modelAnswer: It shows that dead seeds produce no cloudiness, proving the colour change in tube A comes from respiration rather than from the apparatus.

check.stem: A student finds tube A cloudy but tube B slightly cloudy too. Suggest one cause and one fix.
check.modelAnswer: Microbes on unsterilised seeds may be respiring in both tubes; sterilising the set-up and using fresh seeds removes the stray source.

lessons.title: Watching Heat Leave Living Seeds
lessons.opening: Two vacuum flasks hold equal batches of seeds — one boiled dead, one alive and germinating — and thermometers seated among the seeds record whether living respiration warms its surroundings.
keyPoints: Flask A holds boiled seeds; flask B holds germinating seeds.
Each thermometer bulb sits among the seeds it monitors.
Cotton wool seals the flasks and trims heat loss.
The flasks and seeds are sterilised with weak bleach first.
Temperatures are logged at the start and again after 2-3 days.

low.restatement: Only the flask with living seeds warms up; the dead-seed flask stays level.
low.analogy: A compost heap steams on a cold morning — packed living material gives off heat as it works.
low.examPointer: Sterilisation is the marker-winning detail: microbes respire too and would warm both flasks.

medium.restatement: Sterilising removes microbes whose own respiration would otherwise add heat, so any rise can be attributed to the seeds alone.
medium.analogy: Silencing the audience before timing a soloist, so every note you hear belongs to the soloist.
medium.examPointer: Call flask A the killed control: it exposes any room-temperature drift.

check.stem: Why must the seeds and flasks be sterilised with weak bleach?

options.text: So microbes cannot respire and add their own heat to either flask
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Bleach is not a nutrient.
Coat softening is irrelevant to the temperature reading.
Sterilisation has nothing to do with colour.

check.stem: Where should each thermometer bulb sit?

options.text: Among the seeds inside its flask
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: In the room beside the flasks
options.explanation: A room thermometer helps, but the flask reading needs contact with the seeds.
The wall warms and cools differently from the seed mass.

options.text: Under the cotton wool seal only
options.explanation: The wool holds the thermometer; the bulb must reach the seeds.

check.stem: What temperature behaviour is expected in flask A with dead seeds?

options.text: Steady, apart from any drift in the room temperature
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Dead seeds do not respire, so no heat is added.
Insulation minimises loss; no sharp fall is expected.
Flask B warms because its seeds are alive.

check.stem: In the recorded results, what change did the germinating-seed flask show?

options.text: A rise of 5.5 degrees Celsius, from 20.0 to 25.5
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Twenty was the starting temperature, not the rise.
Respiration warms; it does not chill.
Living seeds released enough heat to lift the reading clearly.

check.stem: Why are the flask tops sealed with cotton wool?

options.text: It holds the thermometer in place and reduces heat loss
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It lets oxygen flood in freely
options.explanation: The wool is a plug, not an air valve.
Sterilisation is the bleach step, done beforehand.
Nothing in this set-up absorbs gas.

check.stem: State the temperature change recorded for the germinating-seed flask.
check.modelAnswer: It rose by 5.5 degrees Celsius, from 20.0 to 25.5.

check.stem: Name the solution used to sterilise the seeds and flasks.
check.modelAnswer: A weak bleach solution sterilises them before the run.

check.stem: Explain why a temperature rise in flask A would point to the room, not the seeds.
check.modelAnswer: Because dead seeds cannot respire, any warming there must come from the surroundings, which is why room temperature is monitored alongside.

check.stem: Both flasks drift up by 1 degree, but flask B climbs 5.5 in total. Interpret the numbers.
check.modelAnswer: The shared 1-degree drift reflects the room; the extra 4.5 degrees in flask B is the heat released by its respiring seeds.

lessons.title: Reading Results and Applying CORMS
lessons.opening: The results tables settle each claim — cloudiness only where seeds live, warmth only where seeds respire — and the CORMS prompt turns those observations into a defensible design.
keyPoints: Cloudy limewater after about three hours marks respiring seeds.
Clear limewater in the controls marks the absence of life.
CORMS stands for Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
Repeat runs check that one result is not a fluke.
Indicator volume, seed count and temperature belong in the Same list.

low.restatement: Cloudiness and warmth both track living seeds; CORMS frames how to vary, repeat and measure.
low.analogy: A referee's checklist before awarding a goal: every condition must hold before the result stands.
low.examPointer: Quote the windows exactly: about three hours for limewater, 2-3 days for the heat run.

medium.restatement: CORMS disciplines the design: one changed factor, matched organisms, repeats, measurements at fixed times and controlled conditions elsewhere.
medium.analogy: Photographing two gardens from the same spot at the same hour across several days before claiming one blooms earlier.
medium.examPointer: Tie every CORMS letter to this practical rather than reciting a generic template.

check.stem: In the carbon dioxide set-up, when is the limewater observed?

options.text: After about three hours in the warm environment
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The named window is about three hours.
Days suit the heat-flask run, not this one.
Gas needs time to accumulate and react.

check.stem: What does the letter S in CORMS stand for?

options.text: Same — the factors held constant across tubes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
S is about constancy, not selection.
Sterilisation belongs to the method, not the CORMS letter.
No letter tracks ordering.

check.stem: Which factor belongs in the Change slot for the limewater investigation?

options.text: The tube contents: germinating seeds, dead seeds or beads
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Temperature is held constant, so it belongs in the Same list.
Volume is controlled, not varied.
Nothing about the observer changes between tubes.

check.stem: Why repeat each investigation several times?

options.text: For reliability: one anomalous run should not drive the conclusion
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Repeats answer reliability, not logistics.
Repeats do not warm anything.
Small variation is expected; repeats expose it.

check.stem: Which measurement settles the heat claim, and after how long?

options.text: Thermometer temperature, initially and again after 2-3 days
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
That belongs to the potometer practical.
That belongs to the limewater set-up.
Mass is not recorded in this practical.

check.stem: State the CORMS letters in order.
State one factor kept the same across the three limewater tubes.
check.modelAnswer: The volume of indicator is the same in every tube.

check.stem: Explain why the glass-bead tube strengthens the limewater conclusion.
check.modelAnswer: Because beads occupy volume like seeds but never respire, so a clear tube C rules out the apparatus itself as the source of the cloudiness.

check.stem: Draft the CORMS Change and Measurement entries for testing blowfly larvae instead of seeds.
check.modelAnswer: Change the tube contents to larvae against an empty control, and observe the limewater cloudiness after the same three-hour window.

glossary.definition: Calcium hydroxide solution that turns cloudy when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
A tube or flask run without the living factor, used to expose other causes.
A design prompt: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measurement, Same.
Killing surface microbes with weak bleach so their respiration cannot confuse results.
